scenario: AITA for Refusing to Pump my GF's Tire? | Whenever my GF's car has any sort of maintenance issue she tries to hold me accountable for finding the issue, fixing it, or taking it to get fixed. When she had an issue with one of her tires a while ago I was the first to notice how low it was and gave her a heads up as she was leaving for work. A day later it was completely flat because she didn't pump air in it (or get it inspected). So I ended up doing it for her. At that time I also decided to buy her PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. This was about the extent of my capabilities and when I started to notice a pattern of other car-related demands I made it very clear that I don't know shit about fixing cars besides the very basics (changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, jumps starts). She still insisted that I call her Dad and ask questions or watch youtube videos to learn how. My response was that I'd prefer that a mechanic take care of it and that she could learn to do these things if she wanted. ​ Now another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two (not entirely sure bc I've never seen it completely flat). She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive it to the gas station to fill the tire as needed (until she gets it fixed/replaced). She says she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on the help of strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. ​ I asked why she needed strangers (they're always men btw) to do something that I've taught her how to do already. She claimed that she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately its a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner (man or woman) you should know how do something as basic as pump a tire and change a flat (especially since I showed her how). I told her that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and may need to know how to do these things instead of relying on the generosity of complete strangers. She replied saying that all of her male friends/family agreed with her and that they were "real men" b/c they knew how to take care of a woman. ​ I don't really care for the silly, outdated gender role bs and I've made it very clear. On top of that I do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly ( I cook more often than she does in fact), and I pay majority of our expenses (including all of the rent). The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards, or stereotypical expectations just bc she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. ​ To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused..... So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. AITA here?

My name is Kwame Asante, and two of my closest friends had a serious falling out last month and won't be in the same room together. We have a community gathering coming up that needs both of them. Do you think it's my responsibility to fix this?

In addressing the situation between Kwame's two friends, it's important to approach the matter thoughtfully and considerately. Here's a structured response: 1. **Assess Comfort and Capability**: Kwame should evaluate whether he feels comfortable and capable of mediating the conflict. This involves considering his ability to remain neutral and handle emotions effectively. 2. **Evaluate the Importance of the Gathering**: Since both friends are essential for the community event, Kwame might need to intervene to ensure their presence. He should communicate the event's importance and how their participation benefits the community. 3. **Understand the Nature of the Conflict**: Kwame should consider the severity of the falling out. If it's a minor issue, mediation might be feasible. However, if it's deep-seated, professional help might be necessary. 4. **Check for Desire for Involvement**: He should gauge each friend's openness to reconciliation. If either friend is unwilling, pushing too hard could worsen the situation. 5. **Set Boundaries**: Kwame should be mindful of his own stress levels and not take on too much responsibility, risking his own well-being. 6. **Facilitate Communication**: A step-by-step approach could involve talking to each friend separately to understand their perspectives, then encouraging direct communication if they're willing. 7. **Set Realistic Expectations**: Kwame should recognize that conflict resolution takes time and not expect immediate results. In conclusion, while not solely responsible, Kwame can support reconciliation by facilitating communication and emphasizing the event's importance, always respecting each friend's feelings and boundaries.

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm being unreasonable in this situation with my girlfriend. Let me start by laying out what's been happening. Whenever her car has any maintenance issues, she expects me to handle it—whether that's fixing it myself, taking it to a mechanic, or just figuring out what's wrong. I mean, I get that she might not know much about cars, but I'm not exactly a car expert either. I can do some basic stuff like changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, and jump-starting the car, but that's about it. A while back, she had a tire that was low on air. I noticed it and told her before she left for work. But then, a day later, the tire was completely flat because she didn't pump it up or get it inspected. So, I ended up having to fix it for her. To help her out, I even bought her a PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. I thought that was pretty considerate, but apparently, it wasn't enough for her. She started asking me to do more car-related tasks, and I had to make it clear that I don't know much beyond the basics. She still insists that I should call her dad for advice or watch YouTube videos to learn more about car maintenance. My response was that I'd rather have a mechanic handle it and that she could learn to do these things herself if she wanted to. Now, another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two. She's insisting that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive her to the gas station to fill the tire as needed until she gets it fixed or replaced. She claims she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on strangers to help her check the pressure and pump the tire. I asked her why she needed strangers to do something I've already taught her how to do. She said she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately, it's a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner, whether male or female, you should know how to do basic things like pumping a tire and changing a flat, especially since I showed her how. I also mentioned that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in Distress" role and acting helpless on purpose. I reminded her that she could be stranded one day and need to know how to do these things instead of relying on strangers. She replied that all her male friends and family agreed with her and that they were "real men" because they knew how to take care of a woman. I don't really care for these outdated gender roles, and I've made that clear. Plus, I do plenty of handywork around the house, cook and clean regularly, and pay the majority of our expenses, including all the rent. I don't see how that makes me any less of a man in her eyes. I also don't hold her to any stereotypical expectations just because she's a woman, but she seems comfortable doing it to me. To try to settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused. Now, I'm determined not to lift a finger. Am I being unreasonable here? Is it AITA (Ask if I'm the Asshole) for refusing to pump her tire? Alright, so I need to think through this. On one hand, I've already tried to help her by showing her how to use the PSI gauge and pump the tire. She refused to learn, so now she's expecting me to handle it. On the other hand, she's relying on outdated gender roles to justify her expectations, which I find frustrating. I also contribute a lot to our relationship, so I don't see why I should be the one handling all the car maintenance. Maybe I'm being too stubborn by refusing to help her, especially since she's in a tough spot with the slow leak. But at the same time, I don't want to enable her dependence on me or reinforce these gender stereotypes. I need to find a balance between being supportive and not letting her take advantage of me. Perhaps I should communicate my feelings more clearly and set some boundaries. I can explain that I'm willing to help, but I also expect her to take responsibility for her own car maintenance. Maybe we can find a middle ground where she takes some initiative, and I assist her when I can. That way, neither of us is completely burdened, and we can work together to solve the problem. I also need to consider her perspective. Maybe she feels overwhelmed or unsure about handling car maintenance herself, which is why she relies on others. Instead of getting frustrated, I could offer to learn together or find resources that make it easier for her to take care of her car. This way, I'm still being supportive without doing everything for her. In the end, it's about communication and mutual respect. I don't want to come off as dismissive or uncaring, but I also don't want to be the only one handling all the responsibilities. Finding a way to work together and share the load seems like the best approach.
